extracted.intended_audience: scientists, naturalists, taxonomists, and students of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for forming natural (scientific) classifications, nomenclature, and series-arrangements to best serve general knowledge and particular inductive inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider all varieties with any affinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Can not determine the group in which any one object can most conveniently be placed, without taking into consideration all the varieties of existing objects, all at least which have any degree of affinity with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good classification requires global comparison across all related varieties; you must survey the range of things that have any degree of affinity with an object before fixing its place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing scientific classification on merely simple/perceptible properties
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no property of objects which may not be taken, if we please, as the foundation for a classification ... in our first attempts we are likely to select ... properties which are simple, easily conceived, and perceptible on a first view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple, obvious characters (e.g., corolla shape, number of stamens) may help quick identification but are often ill-suited for scientific classification because they do not support general propositions about the members of the group and may mislead habits of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximize number and importance of common properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The ends of scientific classification are best answered, when the objects are formed into groups respecting which a greater number of general propositions can be made, and those propositions more important, than could be made respecting any other groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer arrangements that allow many and significant general assertions about members of a group; scientific character of a classification is tested by number and importance of shared properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer causal properties or sure marks of many others
rubrics_metrics.description: The properties, therefore, according to which objects are classified, should, if possible, be those which are causes of many other properties; or, at any rate, which are sure marks of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes are preferable because they are the surest and most direct marks and are often the most useful properties to fix attention on. When causes are not diagnostically accessible, select prominent effects that reliably indicate the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select diagnostic marks that correspond to important hidden properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Our natural groups, therefore, must often be founded not on the obvious but on the unobvious properties of things, when these are of greater importance. But in such cases it is essential that there should be some other property or set of properties, more readily recognizable by the observer, which co-exist with, and may be received as marks of, the properties which are the real groundwork of the classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When foundational properties are not directly observable (e.g., internal structure), classification should rely on correlated, observable marks (e.g., external integuments) that serve as practical diagnostics without destructive examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural vs Technical (Artificial) classification test
rubrics_metrics.description: A classification is natural when it corresponds, in the groups which it forms, to the spontaneous tendencies of the mind, by placing together the objects most similar in their general aspect; technical systems arrange by arbitrarily selected circumstances and often group dissimilar objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a classification's scientific merit by whether groups share numerous and important properties (natural) rather than by arbitrary single traits (technical). Natural classifications avoid grouping together objects that present no general resemblance in their aggregate properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take purpose into account when choosing important properties
rubrics_metrics.description: What is here meant by importance? It has reference to the particular end in view; and the same objects, therefore, may admit with propriety of several different classifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different sciences or practical ends require different classifications (e.g., farmer: useful plants vs weeds; geologist: fossils by strata). Choose properties important for the intended inquiry or practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: For general study prefer attributes giving marked individuality
rubrics_metrics.description: When we are studying objects ... for the sake of extending our knowledge of the whole of their properties and relations, we must consider as the most important attributes those which contribute most ... to render the things like one another, and unlike other things; which give to the class composed of them the most marked individuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For broad, non-practical scientific classification, prioritize traits that produce the clearest, most distinctive grouping (largest 'space' of existence) and will be predictive of further undiscovered properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes should recognize distinctions of Kind where present
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the common properties of a true Kind ... are indefinite and inexhaustible ... this principle prescribes that every such classification shall recognize and adopt into itself all distinctions of Kind, which exist among the objects it professes to classify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If distinctions of Kind (deep, pervasive differences) exist among objects, a natural classification must reflect them rather than substituting limited, definite distinctions that do not point to further unknown differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes are determined by characters, not solely by types
rubrics_metrics.description: They are determined by characters, but these are not arbitrary. The problem is, to find a few definite characters which point to the multitude of indefinite ones ... I can not think that a group when formed is determined by the type; that in deciding whether a species belongs to the group, a reference is made to the type, and not to the characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define groups by enumerated characters (diagnostic traits) that indicate deeper similarities. Types (central exemplars) are useful illustrations and guides but should not replace explicit characters as the determiner of membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use types as illustrative centrals, not as definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The class is steadily fixed, though not precisely limited; it is given, though not circumscribed; it is determined, not by a boundary-line without, but by a central point within ... in short, instead of a Definition we have a Type for our director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A type-species or genus can serve as a central exemplar around which similar species cluster; useful for mental representation and for suggesting groups, especially when classifications are for particular inductive inquiries, but do not substitute for character-based definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class constitution: universal characters + most exceptionable characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The class, therefore, is constituted by the possession of all the characters which are universal, and most of those which admit of exceptions. ... It may want any one, or more than one of these characters, and not be excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining a class, require the universal characters and a majority of the common characters; admit a few exceptions when overall resemblance (in known properties) indicates closer affinity to that class than any other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomenclature should convey maximal independent significance
rubrics_metrics.description: A Nomenclature in science ... The only merit which a set of names can have beyond this, is to convey, by the mode of their construction, as much information as possible ... The best ... is when the word can be made to indicate, by its formation, the very properties which it is designed to connote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer names that, through formation or etymology, indicate distinguishing properties. Where this is impracticable, incorporate the proximate natural group's name (binary nomenclature) to signal affinities and economize memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt binary (or ternary if needed) nomenclature to economize names
rubrics_metrics.description: By adding to this the name of the superior genus, we may make the best amends we can for the impossibility of so contriving the name as to express all the distinctive characters ... If even those common characters are so numerous ... we might, instead of a binary, adopt a ternary nomenclature ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hierarchical composition in species names (genus + specific epithet, or genus+family+species when necessary) to encode natural affinities and reduce the number of distinct names to be memorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by series for particular inductive inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: The requisites of a classification intended to facilitate the study of a particular phenomenon, are, first to bring into one class all Kinds of things which exhibit that phenomenon ... and, secondly, to arrange those Kinds in a series according to the degree in which they exhibit it, beginning with those which exhibit most of it, and terminating with those which exhibit least.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When investigating a specific phenomenon, group all kinds showing the phenomenon and order them by degree of manifestation (a series). This arrangement supports inductive methods like Concomitant Variations and aids in detecting causal relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange series to enable Concomitant Variations method
rubrics_metrics.description: We should put the instances, from which the law is to be inductively collected, into the order which is implied in one of the four Methods of Experimental Inquiry discussed ... the fourth Method, that of Concomitant Variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordering instances by the degree of the phenomenon allows observation of covariation (things that increase or diminish together), which is critical for inferring cause-and-effect or common-cause relationships when controlled experiments are impractical.
